content: 1. Hydrogen sulfide gas is periodically released along the Namibian coast. 2. Ocean currents transport oxygen-depleted water to this region, and both chemical and biological processes further reduce the already limited oxygen levels. 3. The sediments on the local seafloor are rich in organic matter. 4. When organic matter decays in an oxygen-poor environment, it can lead to the emission of hydrogen sulfide gas. 5. NASA’s Terra satellite, using the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS), captured a natural-color image of this phenomenon on February 29, 2012. 6. Pale-colored surface waters snake along the Namib Desert coastline, extending approximately 150 kilometers (90 miles). 7. The milky-green hues observed along Namibia’s coast indicate high concentrations of sulfur and low oxygen levels. 8. Such events are not only visually striking but also toxic to local marine organisms. 9. Fish die in these low-oxygen waters; however, their carcasses provide food for birds. 10. Lobsters, attempting to escape the toxic seawater, crawl onto the shore, where they become a food source for local residents. 11. Certain species of foraminifera, which are tiny shelled marine organisms, thrive in the oxygen-depleted sediments of the Namibian seafloor. Phytoplankton 12. On February 18, 2010, phytoplankton swirled across the Arabian Sea, forming thin green ribbons shaped by turbulent eddies. 13. The bloom extended from the shores of Pakistan to the coast of Oman. 14. The washed-out appearance in the upper left of the image is due to sunglint, which is the mirror-like reflection of sunlight off the water. 15. Some of the brightness may also be attributed to blowing dust. 16. Pakistan’s coastal waters exhibit both blue and green hues. 17. These colors are influenced by factors such as phytoplankton and sediment. 18. Phytoplankton blooms in the northern Arabian Sea are strongly affected by seasonal monsoon wind shifts. 19. The Arabian Sea, being landlocked to the north, is less influenced by large-scale ocean circulation and more by monsoon winds. 20. Large phytoplankton blooms occur in summer when strong southwesterly winds mix the water. 21. Winter blooms also occur when northeasterly winds blow offshore. Sediments 22. On December 14, 2008, the shallow waters of the Gulf of Mexico near the Yucatan Peninsula displayed a burst of color, captured by NASA’s Terra satellite using MODIS. 23. The swirls of tan, green, blue, and white are likely caused by sediment in the water. 24. Sediment scatters light, giving the water its distinctive colors. 25. The sediment originates from both land and the seafloor. 26. Some of the coloration may also result from phytoplankton, which are tiny plant-like organisms living in sunlit surface waters. 27. Near the shore, the water appears tan due to rivers carrying dirt from land to the ocean. 28. As the sediment disperses, the water transitions to green and eventually black. 29. To the north, the water appears more blue and white, likely due to sediment from the seafloor. 30. Seafloor sediment, composed of chalky white calcium carbonate from shell-building marine life like coral, gives the water a white or bright blue color. 31. This sediment was likely brought to the surface in shallow waters by strong waves. 32. A few days before the image was taken, strong winds churned the Gulf. 33. The blue-green cloud in the image roughly matches the extent of the shallow continental shelf west of the peninsula. Volcanoes 34. After two months of eruptions and six months of seismic activity, the underwater volcano off the coast of El Hierro appears to be quieting down. 35. A mass of new crust has been forming, rising tens to perhaps hundreds of meters, but it remains far below the ocean surface and does not extend the Canary Island chain. 36. NASA’s Earth Observing-1 (EO-1) satellite, using the Advanced Land Imager (ALI), captured a natural-color image of the island and its offshore eruption on December 16, 2011. 37. The eruption is located about one kilometer south-southwest of the town of La Restinga. 38. The milky green swirls in the Atlantic Ocean are a mixture of steaming lava fragments, rock debris, heated gas, and other volcanic materials carried west and north by currents. 39. Meanwhile, tremors have been occurring on the island’s north side at depths of 17 to 23 kilometers. 40. Red circles mark the locations of three tremors reported on December 18. 41. The white puffs over the island are clouds, not volcanic emissions. 42. El Hierro is a shield volcano growing along the southwestern edge of the ancient El Golfo volcano. 43. El Golfo collapsed approximately 130,000 years ago, but the rugged, reddish-brown terrain of the island reflects its long history of volcanism. 44. According to historical records, El Hierro last erupted in 1793, and the area has the highest concentration of young vents in the Canary Islands. Greenstones 45. Greenstone belts are zones of variably metamorphosed mafic to ultramafic volcanic sequences, often associated with sedimentary rocks, found within Archaean and Proterozoic cratons between granite and gneiss bodies. 46. The name greenstone comes from the green hue imparted by metamorphic minerals within the mafic rocks, such as chlorite and actinolite. 47. These belts can range from several dozen to several thousand kilometers in length and are considered stratigraphic groupings on a continental scale. 48. Greenstone belts are distributed throughout geological history, from Phanerozoic examples like the Franciscan belts of California to Palaeozoic belts in the Lachlan Fold Belt of Eastern Australia, and numerous Proterozoic and Archaean examples. 49. Archaean greenstones are found in regions such as the Slave craton in northern Canada, the Pilbara and Yilgarn cratons in Western Australia, the Gawler craton in South Australia, and the Wyoming craton in the United States. 50. Examples also exist in South and Eastern Africa, including the Kaapvaal craton, as well as in Madagascar, West Africa, Brazil, northern Scandinavia, and the Kola Peninsula. 51. Phanerozoic ophiolite and greenstone belts occur in regions such as the Franciscan Complex of southwestern North America, the Lachlan Fold Belt, the Gympie Terrane of Eastern Australia, and the ophiolite belts of Oman and the Guiana Shield. Meteors 52. The first identification of the OI 5577 Å green line emission was made by Halliday in 1959. 53. This emission is a significant contributor to meteor wake spectra. 54. The emission occurs only in the upper part of the meteor light curve, generally confined to altitudes between 100 and 110 kilometers, and is rare in meteors with velocities below approximately 40 km/s. Meteorites 55. Moldavite is an olive-green or dull greenish vitreous substance, possibly formed by a meteorite impact. 56. It is a type of tektite. 57. Due to its difficult fusibility, extremely low water content, and unique chemical composition, the prevailing consensus among Earth scientists is that moldavites were formed 15 million years ago during the impact of a giant meteorite in present-day Nördlinger Ries. 58. Material melted by the impact cooled while airborne, with most of it falling in central Bohemia, traversed by the Vltava River.
